# Lecture 14 — Motilité gastro-intestina:
# Lecture 14 — Gastrointestinal Motility

## 1. Characteristics of Visceral Smooth Muscle

- Organization in layers: external longitudinal, internal circular, and deep oblique (gastric only).
- The **myenteric plexus of Auerbach** is located between the longitudinal and circular layers (intrinsic innervation). Junctions are diffuse: a varicosity containing neurotransmitter influences multiple muscle fibers.
- Organization of **syncytial type**: muscle fibers conduct excitation via **connexons** (gap junctions), which propagates in a cranio-caudal direction, producing a unitary contraction of the muscle layer.
- **Functional automatism** ensured by pacemaker cells of Cajal (at the level of the myenteric plexus of Auerbach), coupled to smooth muscle fibers by gap junctions.
- **Basal tone (myogenic mechanism)**: permanent contractile state based on oscillations of the resting potential around -50 mV.
- The control of contraction is both nervous and hormonal.

## 2. Types of Gastrointestinal Movements
[[visual:phys/gi-motility]]


- **Movements associated with digestion and absorption**: tonic (contraction of digestive sphincters, preventing premature passage of intestinal content), segmental (mixing), peristaltic (propulsion).
- **Movements associated with the fasting state**: gastric (peristaltic contractions of "hunger"), intestinal (migrating motor complexes, basis of periodic peristaltic contractions for complete gastrointestinal evacuation).

### 2.1 Peristaltic Movements
- Characteristics of tubular syncytial smooth muscle (bile ducts, glandular ducts, ureters, etc.).
- Propel intestinal content over a distance of 5-10 cm, from one point to the nearest point, in a cranio-caudal direction.
- Triggered by: mechanical distension of the digestive tube, chemical/physical irritation of the intestinal mucosa, intense parasympathetic stimulation. Coordinated by the myenteric plexus of Auerbach, required for effective peristaltic activity.
- **Starling's law of the intestine (peristaltic reflex)**: distension of a segment triggers 1) a contractile wave (ACh/substance P), 2-3 cm in length, proximal to the point of distension, and 2) a receptive relaxation wave (NO/VIP) caudal to the point of distension — peristaltic movements thus direct toward the anus.

### 2.2 Segmental Movements
- Series of alternating concentric contractions followed by relaxation; a new contraction occurs between two previously contractile segments.
- Cause fragmentation of intestinal content into mixing segments and contractile segments for limited bidirectional propulsion.
- The frequency is characteristic of each intestinal segment (local pacemaker) and progresses to allow local propulsion.

## 3. Mechanisms of Control of Digestive Tract Activity
[[visual:phys/gi-control]]

### 3.1 Intrinsic Nervous Mechanism (Enteric Nervous System, ENS)
- Neuronal network located in the intestinal wall from the esophagus to the anus: **myenteric plexus of Auerbach** and **submucous plexus of Meissner**.
- Comprises sensory neurons (mechano- and chemoreceptors), motor neurons (glandular cells and muscle layers). Establishes connections with most vegetative motor fibers (sympathetic + parasympathetic).
- Roles: ensures functional autonomy of motor and secretory digestive control; establishes connections with the CNS via the peripheral autonomic nervous system (**gut-brain axis**: effect of emotions/anxiety on motility, perception of distension, satiety, nausea, pain); mediates local reflexes initiated by the extrinsic nervous mechanism (long vago-vagal reflexes: mechanical distension, local irritating factors, products of lipid/protein digestion).
- **Plexus of Auerbach** (between the longitudinal and circular layers): controls motility (muscle layers, digestive sphincters).
- **Plexus of Meissner** (submucous): controls secretion and absorption, local blood flow, motility of the mucosal muscle layer.
- Principal neurotransmitter: ACh (stimulatory effect); noradrenaline and NO (inhibitory effect). Principal co-transmitters: substance P, VIP.

### 3.2 Extrinsic Nervous Mechanism
- **Parasympathetic innervation**: bulbar origin (vagus nerves X) and lateral horns S2-S4 (pelvic nerves). NT: ACh, muscarinic receptors. Role: contraction of the muscle layer, relaxation of digestive sphincters, stimulation of digestive secretion, vasodilation. The vagus nerve (75% afferent fibers, 25% efferent, long vago-vagal reflexes) innervates the stomach, small intestine, and right half of the colon; pelvic nerves innervate the left half of the colon and rectum.
- **Sympathetic innervation**: origin lateral horns T5-L3 → paravertebral ganglia → sympathetic nerves. NT: noradrenaline, adrenergic receptors. Role: relaxation of the muscle layer, contraction of sphincters, inhibition of digestive secretion, vasoconstriction. Distribution: celiac plexus (T5-T9, stomach/duodenum), superior mesenteric plexus (T9-L1, small intestine/right half of colon), inferior mesenteric plexus (T12-L3, left half of colon/rectum).

### 3.3 Endocrine and Paracrine Mechanisms
- **Gastrointestinal hormones** (endocrine cells of the digestive mucosa):
  - **Gastrin** (stomach, duodenum): gastric acid secretion↑, gastrointestinal motility↑.
  - **CCK** (duodenum, jejunum): gastric motility↓, pancreatic enzyme secretion↑, bile duct motility↑.
  - **Secretin** (duodenum): pancreatic/biliary HCO₃⁻ secretion↑, gastric acid secretion↓, gastrointestinal motility↓.
  - **Motilin** (duodenum, jejunum): intestinal motility↑.
- **Biogenic amines (paracrine mechanism)**:
  - **Somatostatin** (stomach, intestine): inhibits the release of gastrointestinal hormones (gastrin → gastric secretion/motility↓; secretin → pancreatic secretion↓; motilin → intestinal motility↓).
  - **Histamine** (stomach): gastric acid secretion↑.
  - **Serotonin** (intestine): intestinal motility and secretion↑.

## 4. Mastication
[[visual:phys/mastication-reflex]]

- **Definition**: mechanical processing and mixing with saliva of food introduced into the mouth → formation of the **food bolus**.
- Active component: teeth, mandible, temporomandibular joint, masticatory muscles (nerve V), tongue muscles (nerve XII), oro-facial muscles (nerve VII). Functional roles: teeth (grinding, occlusal surface), masticatory muscles (mandibular movements, occlusion), tongue (propulsion of food onto the grinding surface), oro-facial muscles (retention of saliva and food in the mouth).
- **Masticatory reflex (myotatic)**: succession of unconditional reflexes of mandibular depression/elevation, sustained by voluntary control.
  1. **Myotatic reflex**: voluntary mouth opening → stretching of the masseter muscle → Ia sensory fibers of nerve V → pontine motor nucleus of nerve V → somatic motor fibers of nerve V → masseter contraction → mandibular elevation.
  2. **Inverse myotatic reflex**: masseter contraction → stretching of the Golgi tendon organ → Ib sensory fibers of nerve V → pontine motor nucleus → masseter relaxation → mandibular depression.
- Voluntary cortical control: frontal area 4 → cortico-nuclear tract → pontine motor nucleus of V (mandibular movements), VII (oro-facial coordination), XII (lingual coordination).
- **Functional value of mastication**: 1) digestive (mechanical/chemical food preparation); 2) trophic for the oral cavity (development of facial bones, stimulation of salivary secretion, oral self-cleaning, olfactory/gustatory perception); 3) trophic for the digestive tube (mechanical integrity, reflex stimulation of digestive secretion and motility).

## 5. Swallowing
[[visual:phys/swallowing]]

- **Definition**: mechanical process in 3 stages (buccal, pharyngeal, esophageal) moving the food bolus from the mouth to the stomach via the pharynx and esophagus.

### 5.1 Buccal Stage (≈0.3 s, voluntary)
- Elevation of the tongue tip → elevation of the anterior part of the tongue (contraction of lingual muscles) → widening of the buccopharyngeal isthmus (relaxation of the pillars of the soft palate, elevation of the palatal folds) → pharyngeal suction of the food bolus (negative pharyngeal pressure) → passage through the buccopharyngeal isthmus.

### 5.2 Pharyngeal Stage (1-2 s, automatic, involuntary)
- Closure of the oral cavity (closure of the buccopharyngeal isthmus, prolonged contraction of the tongue and soft palate muscles).
- Closure of the larynx (laryngeal elevation, glottic narrowing, epiglottis covering the glottis).
- Closure of the nasal cavity.
- Opening of the esophagus, contraction of pharyngeal muscles — propulsive pressure of 70-100 cm H₂O.

### 5.3 Esophageal Stage (5-7 s, involuntary)
- Transient relaxation of the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) → propagation of the food bolus by peristaltic waves → transient receptive relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and stomach.
- **Primary peristaltic waves**: triggered by vagal mechanism, begin with UES relaxation induced by the food bolus, end with receptive relaxation of the LES.
- **Secondary peristaltic waves**: triggered by the myenteric plexus of Auerbach, begin at the level of esophageal distension when the primary wave has not been sufficient to advance the food bolus.
- **UES**: tonic contraction, pressure 50 mmHg — prevents air entry into the esophagus (aerophagia) and regurgitation/laryngeal aspiration.
- **LES**: tonic contraction, pressure 20 mmHg — temporarily arrests bolus progression, prevents gastroesophageal reflux (reflux esophagitis if defective).

### 5.4 Regulation of Swallowing
- **Intrinsic nervous mechanism**: myenteric plexus of Auerbach — inhibits the respiratory center, inhibits the masticatory center, triggers reflexes salivary/lacrimal/vasomotor associated with swallowing of a large food bolus.
- **Extrinsic nervous mechanism**: bulbar swallowing center — coordinates middle and lower esophageal peristalism and LES. Reflex zones: buccopharyngeal isthmus stimulated by salivary particles/moist swallowing material; mechanical esophageal distension. Nerves V, IX, X (V → masseter muscles, VII → mimetic muscles, XII → lingual muscles, IX → pharyngeal muscles, X → esophageal muscles).

## 6. Motor Functions of the Stomach
[[visual:phys/gastric-motility]]

### 6.1 Hunger Contractions
- Characterize the fasting state, occur 12-24 h after complete gastric emptying.
- Rhythmic peristaltic contractions in the body of the stomach that merge into a continuous tetanic contraction lasting 2-3 min.
- In prolonged fasting, maximum intensity at 3-4 days, then progressive weakening.
- Favored by hypoglycemia: gastric excitability ("hunger cramps"), stimulation of ghrelin release by the mucosa of the pyloric antrum → stimulation of the hypothalamic hunger center.

### 6.2 Gastric Storage Function
- **Receptive relaxation**: adjustment of muscle tone to gastric content by vago-vagal reflex + myenteric plexus of Auerbach; transient relaxation of the proximal region of the stomach during passage of the food bolus through the UES.
- Gastric distension up to 1000-1500 mL without increase in intragastric pressure. Food remains ~1 h in the stomach, allowing stratification of gastric content in the order defined for evacuation and time needed for gastric digestion.

### 6.3 Contractile Activity Associated with Gastric Mixing
- **Tonic contractions**: contraction of longitudinal fibers, intragastric pressure 6-10 cm H₂O, movement of food toward the pylorus, gastric evacuation of liquids.
- **Peristaltic contractions (retropulsive)**: contraction of circular fibers, begin in the upper half of the stomach, frequency 3-4 c/min generated by the gastric pacemaker (body of stomach), propagate toward the pylorus with decreasing intensity insufficient to overcome resistance of the pyloric sphincter. Roles: 1) return of gastric content toward the pyloric antrum → fragmentation of solid content into small particles; 2) prevention of duodeno-gastric reflux.

### 6.4 Contractile Activity Associated with Gastric Emptying
- **Propulsive peristaltic movements**: exert a pressure of 50-70 cm H₂O ("pyloric pump") that overcomes the resistance of the pyloric sphincter. Pyloric sphincter relaxed by the vagus nerve (ACh) and plexus of Auerbach (NO/VIP). Intermittent evacuation in small volumes (1-3 mL) of gastric chyme allows neutralization of duodenal acidity and nutrient digestion at the duodenal level. Complete evacuation in 3-4 h.
- Receptive relaxation of the duodenal bulb allowing accumulation of gastric chyme in the duodenum.

### 6.5 Regulation of Gastric Emptying
- **Extrinsic nervous mechanism (vagus)**: gastric distension → stimulatory.
- **Intrinsic nervous mechanism (plexus of Auerbach)**: gastric distension → stimulatory; duodenal distension and hypertonia → inhibitory.
- **Endocrine mechanism (negative feedback)**: products of protein digestion at the gastric level → stimulatory (gastrin secretion); duodenal pH (3.5) → inhibitory (secretin secretion); products of lipid digestion at the duodenal level → inhibitory (CCK secretion).

## 7. Motor Function of the Small Intestine
[[visual:phys/small-intestine-motility]]

### 7.1 Mixing and Absorption Movements
- Movements of the muscle fibers of the villi: relaxation favors intestinal absorption, contraction propels villous content toward the submucosal circulation.
- Movements of the muscularis mucosae: folds of the intestinal mucosa, mixing movements near the absorption surface.
- **Segmental movements**: progressive frequency allowing local propulsion of intestinal content, mixing of intestinal chyme; characteristic frequency per segment (duodenum 12/min, jejunum 10/min, ileum 6-8/min).

### 7.2 Propulsive Movements Associated with Evacuation
- **Migrating motor complex (MMC)** = periodic myoelectric activity: occurs in fasting state and post-absorption, periodic contractions at intervals of approximately 90 min, from the pyloric antrum to the colon. Stimulated by motilin, inhibited by erythromycin. Ensures complete evacuation of the small intestine (undigested food, secretions, bacteria, epithelial cells), inhibits bacterial migration from the colon to the small intestine, allows intestinal passage in 3-5 h. Can occur at any level of the small intestine, movement toward the anus.

### 7.3 Regulation of Small Intestine Motility
- Intrinsic nervous mechanism (primary role, functional autonomy); extrinsic nervous mechanism (secondary role, parasympathetic stimulatory, sympathetic inhibitory); endocrine mechanism (minor role, gastrin/CCK/motilin stimulatory, secretin inhibitory).
- **Mechanical distension — gastrointestinal effects**: gastro-enteric reflex (gastric distension increases small intestine motility, chyme progresses to the ileocecal valve); gastro-ileal reflex (new gastric distension increases ileal motility and relaxes the ileocecal sphincter, pushing chyme into the cecum).

## 8. Motor Function of the Large Intestine

- **Receptive relaxation at the cecal level**: allows accumulation of intestinal chyme without increase in intestinal pressure.
- **Segmental movements (haustra)**: contractions combining circular and longitudinal fibers (tænia), frequency 3-10 c/h, divide the intestinal lumen into ovoid segments = **haustra**.
- **Anti-propulsive movements (inverse peristalism)**: retention of content at the proximal colon level, facilitating absorption of NaCl and water. Mixing and absorption function specific to the **proximal colon**.
- **Temporary storage function**, specific to the **distal colon**: allows intestinal passage of 8-15 h. Haustra: frequency 11-17 c/h. The decreasing frequency of segmental movements (local propulsion) allows complete fluid absorption in the proximal colon.
- **"Mass transport" movements**: very strong grouped peristaltic contractions, 1-3 times/day, ensure complete colon evacuation, strongly influenced by emotions and conditioned excitatory stimuli.

## 9. Defecation
[[visual:phys/colon-defecation]]

- **Definition**: evacuation of rectal content, by recto-sphincteric reflex and voluntary control.
- **Intrinsic myenteric reflex**: reduced effectiveness.
- **Extrinsic parasympathetic reflex**: mechanical distension of the rectum, intra-rectal pressure at 20 mmHg ("call to defecate") → spinal anal center (lateral horns S2-S4) → pelvic nerves → peristaltic waves in the colon and rectum, propulsion of rectal content toward the anus, relaxation of the internal anal sphincter.
- **Temporization of defecation**: 1) voluntary contraction of the external anal sphincter; 2) adaptive relaxation of the rectum (myenteric plexus of Auerbach + sympathetic fibers) — anti-peristaltic rectal movements, contraction of the internal anal sphincter, accumulation of feces (intra-rectal pressure 40-50 mmHg) via the spinal anal center (lateral horns L2-L4) and hypogastric nerves.
- **Voluntary control**: complete from the 15th month of life. Cerebral cortex → rectal contraction + relaxation of internal sphincter (anterior horns S2-S4) and voluntary contraction/relaxation of external sphincter (pudendal nerves). The act of defecation also involves deep inhalation + glottic closure, contraction of abdominal muscles, relaxation of the pelvic floor.

## Points to Retain
- Digestive smooth muscle is of unitary syncytial type, with its own automatism (Cajal cells) and superimposed nervous/hormonal control.
- Three control mechanisms: intrinsic nervous (ENS, functional autonomy), extrinsic nervous (parasympathetic stimulatory, sympathetic inhibitory), endocrine/paracrine (gastrin, CCK, secretin, motilin, somatostatin).
- Swallowing: 3 stages (voluntary buccal, involuntary pharyngeal and esophageal), bulbar coordination, primary/secondary peristaltic waves.
- Stomach: receptive relaxation (storage), retropulsive contractions (mixing), pyloric pump (emptying), regulation by gastrin/secretin/CCK.
- Small intestine: segmentation (mixing, digestion/absorption) vs migrating motor complex (evacuation in fasting state, stimulated by motilin).
- Colon: haustra and anti-propulsive movements (proximal, absorption) vs storage and mass transport (distal, evacuation).
- Defecation: involuntary parasympathetic reflex, temporized by complete voluntary cortical control from 15 months.
# Muscles du membre inférieur\n\nLes mus:
# Muscles of the Lower Limb

The muscles of the lower limb are classified into 4 regional groups: iliac region, thigh/buttock, leg, foot.

## A. Muscles of the Iliac Region
[[visual:anat/iliac-muscles]]

| Muscle | Origin | Insertion | Innervation | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Psoas major** | Intervertebral discs and bodies T12-L5, lumbar transverse processes, tendinous arches | Lesser trochanter of femur | Ventral branches L2-L4 | Main flexor of thigh at hip; with femur fixed, flexes trunk (lying to sitting transition) |
| **Psoas minor** (present in ~50%) | Disc T12-L1 | Iliopectineal eminence | Branch of L1 | Weak flexor of trunk |
| **Iliacus** | Iliac fossa, internal lip of iliac crest | Fuses with psoas major at lesser trochanter | Femoral nerve | With psoas (iliopsoas): flexion of thigh and lumbar spine |

## B. Muscles of the Thigh and Buttock
[[visual:anat/thigh-compartments]]

### B.1 Anterior Muscles of the Thigh
[[visual:anat/thigh-anterior]]
- **Sartorius**: the longest muscle of the body; anterior superior iliac spine → medial surface of tibia. Femoral nerve. Flexes hip and knee, adducts and laterally rotates thigh (tailor position).
- **Quadriceps femoris** (4 heads, all terminate by quadriceps tendon → patella → patellar tendon → tibial tuberosity; all innervated by femoral nerve; all knee extensors):
  - Rectus femoris: anterior inferior iliac spine; only bi-articular head, also flexes hip.
  - Vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius: origin on femur (intertrochanteric line, linea aspera, diaphysis).
- **Articularis genu**: detached from vastus intermedius; pulls synovial membrane upward during knee extension.

### B.2 Medial Muscles (Adductors)
[[visual:anat/thigh-adductors]]
| Muscle | Insertion | Innervation | Particularity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Gracilis** | Medial surface of tibia | Anterior branch of obturator nerve | Only adductor not attached to femur; adductor + knee flexor + medial rotator of leg |
| **Pectineus** | Line from lesser trochanter to linea aspera | Femoral nerve (anterior fibres) + obturator nerve (posterior fibres) | Dual innervation |
| **Adductor longus** | Middle third of linea aspera | Anterior branch of obturator nerve | Powerful adductor and medial rotator |
| **Adductor brevis** | Line from lesser trochanter to linea aspera | Anterior branch of obturator nerve | — |
| **Adductor magnus** | Adductor portion (ischiopubic branch) + ischiocavernosus portion (ischial tuberosity) | Obturator nerve (adductor portion) + tibial nerve (ischiocavernosus portion) | Composite muscle; ischiocavernosus portion is a weak hip extensor |

### B.3 Muscles of the Gluteal Region
[[visual:anat/gluteal-muscles]]
| Muscle | Innervation | Main Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gluteus maximus** | Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1-S2) | Hip extensor and lateral rotator; aids sitting to standing |
| **Gluteus medius** | Superior gluteal nerve (L5, S1) | Hip abductor and medial rotator; stabilizes pelvis during gait |
| **Gluteus minimus** | Superior gluteal nerve | Hip abductor and medial rotator |
| **Tensor fasciae latae** | Superior gluteal nerve | Supports femur on tibia in standing position |
| **Piriformis** | Ventral branches S1-S2 | Lateral rotator of hip |
| **Obturator internus** | Nerve to obturator internus (L5-S1) | Lateral rotator of hip |
| **Gemellus superior** | Nerve to obturator internus | Lateral rotator |
| **Gemellus inferior** | Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4-S1) | Lateral rotator |
| **Quadratus femoris** | Nerve to quadratus femoris | Lateral rotator |
| **Obturator externus** | Posterior branch of obturator nerve | Lateral rotator |

### B.4 Hamstring Muscles (Posterior Thigh)
[[visual:anat/hamstrings]]
[[visual:anat/thigh-muscles]]
Common characteristics: all originate from ischial tuberosity, insert on a leg bone, are innervated by tibial portion of sciatic nerve, flex knee and extend hip, and cross 2 joints (hip and knee).
- **Semitendinosus** → medial surface of tibia (behind sartorius and gracilis).
- **Semimembranosus** → medial condyle of tibia (posterior surface).
- **Biceps femoris** (long head: ischial tuberosity, tibial nerve; short head: linea aspera, common fibular nerve) → head of fibula.

## C. Muscles of the Leg (3 Compartments)
[[visual:anat/leg-compartments]]

### C.a Anterior Compartment (Extensor)
[[visual:anat/leg-anterior]]
All innervated by deep fibular nerve, all dorsiflexors of ankle. All originate from fibula except tibialis anterior (originates from tibia).
- **Tibialis anterior**: chief dorsiflexor; also inverts foot.
- **Extensor hallucis longus**, **Extensor digitorum longus**, **Fibularis tertius**: dorsiflexion ± toe extension ± eversion (fibularis tertius).

### C.b Lateral Compartment
[[visual:anat/leg-lateral]]
- **Fibularis longus** and **fibularis brevis**: superficial fibular nerve; evert foot (fibularis longus is the main evertor).

### C.c Posterior Compartment
[[visual:anat/leg-posterior]]
- **Superficial group** (tibial nerve): **Gastrocnemius** (2 femoral heads) + **soleus** (together form triceps surae, Achilles tendon → calcaneus, powerful plantar flexors); **plantaris** (weak accessory plantar flexor).
- **Deep group** (tibial nerve): **Popliteus** (unlocks knee by lateral rotation of femur at start of flexion); **Flexor digitorum longus**; **Flexor hallucis longus**; **Tibialis posterior** (main invertor of foot).

## D. Muscles of the Foot
[[visual:anat/foot-muscles]]
- **Extrinsic**: tendons of leg muscles extending into the foot (eversion, inversion, plantar/dorsal flexion).
- **Intrinsic**: located within foot, responsible for fine toe movements; distributed on **dorsum** of foot (short extensor of toes, short extensor of hallux) and **sole** of foot (plantar intrinsic muscles, extrinsic and intrinsic combined).

## Key Points to Remember
- Quadriceps femoris (4 heads) is the only knee extensor group, all innervated by femoral nerve.
- Hamstring muscles (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris) are all knee flexors and hip extensors, innervated by tibial nerve (except short head of biceps femoris, common fibular nerve).
- Anterior compartment of leg dorsiflexes (deep fibular nerve), posterior compartment plantarflexes (tibial nerve), lateral compartment everts (superficial fibular nerve).
- Triceps surae (gastrocnemius + soleus) forms calcaneal tendon (Achilles tendon).
# Articulations du membre inférieur — Ha:
# Articulations of the Lower Limb — Hip and Knee

## 1. The Coxofemoral Joint (Hip)

### 1.1 General Overview
[[visual:anat/hip-overview]]
- **Synovial spheroid joint (ball-and-socket joint)**, formed by the reception of the **head of the femur** into the cup-shaped cavity of the **acetabulum** (cotyle).
- Primary functions: to support the weight of the body in standing position, and to transmit to the femoral head the forces generated by movements of the trunk during walking.

### 1.2 Articular Surfaces
- **Head of the femur**: forms more than half a sphere, entirely covered with hyaline cartilage except at one point, the **fovea capitis**, where the round ligament (ligamentum teres) is inserted.
- **Acetabulum** ("vinegar cup"): presents three elements — a **semilunar surface** shaped like a horseshoe (the only articular part, covered with cartilage), the **acetabular notch** and the **acetabular fossa** (non-articular). The **acetabular labrum (cotyloid lip)** increases the depth of the acetabulum.

### 1.3 Ligaments of the Hip
[[visual:anat/hip-joint]]
- **Articular capsule**: dense and resistant fibrous sac. On the hip bone, it attaches 5–6 mm beyond the acetabular margin; on the femur, it attaches anteriorly to the intertrochanteric line and posteriorly approximately 1 cm anterior to the intertrochanteric crest. It is thicker superiorly and anteriorly (where maximum resistance is required), thinner inferiorly and posteriorly. It comprises circular and longitudinal fibres.
- **Iliofemoral ligament** (Bigelow's Y ligament): the most resistant of the hip ligaments, located anterior to the joint; attaches superiorly to the anterior inferior iliac spine and divides into two fascicles terminating on the intertrochanteric line.
- **Pubofemoral ligament (pubocapsular)**: from the obturator crest and superior pubic ramus, blending with the capsule and the vertical fascicle of the iliofemoral ligament.
- **Ischiofemoral ligament (ischiocapsular)**: triangular band of resistant fibres arising from the ischium, posteriorly and inferiorly to the acetabulum.
- **Transverse acetabular ligament**: portion of the labrum devoid of cartilage, which crosses the acetabular notch and transforms it into a foramen for the passage of nutrient vessels.
- **Acetabular labrum (glenoid)**: fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the circumference of the acetabulum, forming a complete circle with the transverse ligament.
- **Ligamentum teres femoris (round ligament)**: flattened triangular band, implanted by its apex in the fovea capitis of the femur, its base on both margins of the acetabular notch.

### 1.4 Synovial Membrane
- Lines the internal face of the fibrous capsule, the intracapsular portion of the femoral neck, both faces of the labrum, the transverse ligament, the ligamentum teres and the fat in the acetabular fossa.

### 1.5 Muscles Associated with the Hip
- **Anterior**: psoas major and iliacus (separated from the capsule by a bursa).
- **Superior**: reflected head of the rectus femoris, gluteus minimus (adherent to the capsule).
- **Medial**: obturator externus, pectineus.
- **Posterior**: piriformis, superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus, obturator externus, quadratus femoris.

### 1.6 Vascularization and Innervation
- **Arteries**: obturator artery, medial circumflex femoral artery, superior and inferior gluteal arteries.
- **Nerves**: articular branches from the sacral plexus, sciatic nerve and obturator nerve.

### 1.7 Movements
- Multiaxial joint: **flexion–extension** (transverse axis), **abduction–adduction** (anteroposterior axis), **medial and lateral rotation** (vertical axis), **circumduction** (combination of the above).

## 2. The Knee Joint
[[visual:anat/knee-joint]]

### 2.1 General Overview
- The largest and most complex joint in the body; it is the principal weight-bearing joint.
- Formerly described as a simple **hinge joint (ginglymus)**, it is actually composed of **three joints in one**: two condylar joints (between each femoral condyle and the meniscus/corresponding tibial condyle) and one femoropatellar joint (partially plane/arthrodial).

### 2.2 Articular Surfaces
- Articular surfaces of the medial and lateral femoral condyles, trochlear surface of the femur, articular surface of the patella, articular surfaces of the medial and lateral tibial condyles.

### 2.3 Ligaments of the Knee
- **Articular capsule**: thin fibrous sac, deficient anteriorly (replaced by the patella, quadriceps, patellar retinaculums and patellar ligament). Attaches approximately 0.5–1 cm from the articular margins; anteriorly, it is pierced by the suprapatellar bursa; posteriorly, attached to the intercondylar line; laterally, it encloses the origin of the popliteus. On the tibia, it is deficient anteriorly at the level of the tibial tuberosity (insertion of the patellar ligament) and presents posteriorly a hiatus for the tendon of the popliteus.
- **Synovial membrane**: lines the fibrous capsule; extends anteriorly above the patella as the **suprapatellar bursa**, posteriorly forms a pouch around the cruciate ligaments.
- **Medial and lateral menisci**: crescent-shaped fibrocartilaginous laminae that deepen the surfaces of the tibial plateau. Thick, convex peripheral border, attached to the capsule; thin, concave inner border, free. Each meniscus covers approximately the two-thirds peripheral portions of the corresponding tibial articular surface.
  - **Medial meniscus**: nearly semicircular, anterior extremity fine, attached to the anterior intercondylar fossa (anterior to the ACL), posterior extremity fixed to the posterior intercondylar fossa.
  - **Lateral meniscus**: nearly circular, covers a broader portion of the articular surface, anterior extremity attached anterior to the intercondylar eminence (near the ACL, with which it fuses).
- **Patellar ligament** (anterior ligament): central portion of the common tendon of the quadriceps femoris, from the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity.
- **Tibial collateral ligament (medial collateral ligament)**: broad, flat and membranous band, from the medial femoral condyle (below the adductor tubercle) to the medial condyle and medial face of the tibia. Crossed by the tendons of the pes anserinus (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus) via a bursa; intimately adherent to the medial meniscus.
- **Fibular collateral ligament (lateral collateral ligament)**: resistant, rounded fibrous cord, from the lateral femoral condyle to the head of the fibula; covered by the tendon of the biceps femoris; without attachment to the lateral meniscus.
- **Cruciate ligaments**: two thick, resistant fibrous bands linking the femur and tibia directly, intracapsular but extrasynovial, crossing in an X — hence their name. They ensure **anteroposterior stability** of the knee.
  - **Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)**: from the depression anterior to the intercondylar eminence of the tibia (blended with the anterior extremity of the lateral meniscus) towards the lateral femoral condyle (posterolateral part).
  - **Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)**: more resistant, shorter and less oblique than the ACL; from the posterior intercondylar fossa of the tibia towards the medial femoral condyle (anterolateral part).
- **Oblique popliteal ligament**: broad, flat fibrous band, fascicle arising from the tendon of the semimembranosus; forms part of the floor of the popliteal fossa, on which the popliteal artery rests.
- **Transverse ligament of the knee**: links the convex anterior border of the lateral meniscus to the anterior extremity of the medial meniscus; of variable thickness, sometimes absent.
- **Coronary ligaments**: simple portions of the capsule linking the periphery of each meniscus to the tibial plateau.

### 2.4 Relations of the Knee
- **Anterior**: quadriceps femoris.
- **Lateral**: tendons of the biceps femoris, popliteus, common fibular nerve.
- **Medial**: sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus, semimembranosus.
- **Posterior**: popliteal vessels, tibial nerve, popliteus, plantaris, medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius, lymph nodes, fat.

### 2.5 Vascularization and Innervation
- **Arteries**: superior genicular artery (branch of the femoral), genicular branches of the popliteal, recurrent branches of the anterior tibial, descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral (branch of the deep femoral).
- **Nerves**: branches of the obturator, femoral, tibial and common fibular nerves.

### 2.6 Movements
- **Flexion and extension** (principal/active movements).
- **Medial and lateral rotation** (associated movements, possible only with the knee flexed).

## Key Points to Remember
- The hip is a multiaxial ball-and-socket joint; the knee combines two condylar joints and one femoropatellar joint.
- The iliofemoral ligament (Bigelow) is the most resistant ligament of the hip; the cruciate ligaments (intracapsular, extrasynovial) ensure anteroposterior stability of the knee.
- The menisci (medial semicircular, lateral nearly circular) deepen the tibial plateau and move with knee movements.
- Knee: flexion–extension = principal movements; rotations = associated movements, only possible in flexion.
# Paroi abdominale antéro-latérale\n\n##:
# Anterolateral Abdominal Wall

## 1. Boundaries
- The anterolateral abdominal wall is a musculoaponeurotic structure confined to the anterior and lateral surfaces of the abdomen.
- **Boundaries**: superiorly the xiphoid process and costal margins; inferiorly the anterior part of the iliac crest, inguinal ligament, pubic tubercle, pubic crest and pubic symphysis; laterally, the midaxillary line separates it from the posterior abdominal wall.

## 2. Layers of the wall, from superficial to deep
1. **Skin**.
2. **Superficial fascia**: single layer over most of the wall, but divisible into two layers near the groin — the **fascia of Camper** (superficial fatty layer) and the **fascia of Scarpa** (deep membranous layer, fibroelastic type).
3. **External oblique muscle** (most superficial laterally).
4. **Rectus abdominis** (most superficial medially).
5. **Internal oblique muscle**.
6. **Transversus abdominis**.
7. **Transversalis fascia**.

## 3. The three flat muscles
[[visual:anat/abdominal-wall]]

### 3.1 External oblique muscle
- **Origin**: eight fleshy digitations from the external surfaces of the eight lower ribs; fibres oriented inferiorly and medially.
- **Insertion**: the most posterior fibres descend vertically to the anterior third of the external lip of the iliac crest (free posterior border of the muscle); the remaining fibres terminate in a broad aponeurosis inserted on the **linea alba**, from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis. The thickened and rolled-up free inferior border of the aponeurosis forms the **inguinal ligament**.
- **Linea alba**: medial fibrous structure, from the xiphoid to the pubic symphysis, formed by fusion of the aponeuroses of the anterior wall muscles.
- **Innervation**: ventral branches of the last six thoracic nerves (T7-T12).

### 3.2 Internal oblique muscle
- Smaller and thinner than the external oblique; situated deep to it.
- **Origin**: lateral two-thirds of the superior surface of the inguinal ligament; anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest (intermediate zone); thoracolumbar fascia. Fibres oriented superiorly and medially (perpendicular to those of the external oblique).
- **Insertion**: the majority of fibres terminate in an aponeurosis inserted on the 7th, 8th and 9th costal cartilages and on the linea alba. The most posterior fibres insert on the inferior border of the three lower ribs. The inferior fibres, arched over the inguinal canal, descend to insert on the pubic crest and pectineal line, fusing with fibres from the transversus abdominis to form the **conjoint tendon**.
- **Innervation**: T7-T12 and L1, via the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (lumbar plexus).

### 3.3 Transversus abdominis
- The deepest of the three flat muscles; fibres predominantly horizontal/transverse.
- **Origin**: lateral third of the superior surface of the inguinal ligament; anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest (internal lip); thoracolumbar fascia; internal surfaces of the six lower ribs and their costal cartilages.
- **Insertion**: the inguinal fibres arch posteriorly to form the roof of the inguinal canal then descend medially to form an aponeurosis fusing with that of the internal oblique (conjoint tendon), inserted on the pubic crest and medial part of the pubic pecten. The majority of fibres terminate in an aponeurosis inserted on the linea alba.
- **Innervation**: T7-T12 and L1, via the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.

## 4. Structures derived from the flat muscles
[[visual:anat/inguinal-region]]
1. **Inguinal ligament** (of Poupart): free inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis, stretched between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle.
2. **Lacunar ligament** (of Gimbernat): portion of the external oblique aponeurosis reflected posteriorly and laterally, attached to the pectineal line; concave base forming the medial limit of the femoral ring; apex corresponding to the pubic tubercle.
3. **Conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis)**: fusion of the lower aponeurotic fibres of the internal oblique and transversus, arched over the spermatic cord, inserted on the pubic crest and medial pectineal line.
4. **Cremaster muscle**: muscular loops derived from the lower arched fibres of the internal oblique, forming the covering of the spermatic cord and testis.
5. **Reflected inguinal ligament** (of Colles): triangular layer of tendons, expansion of the lacunar ligament and inferior pillar of the superficial inguinal ring, passing posterior to the spermatic cord.
6. **Cooper's ligament** (pectineal): resistant fibrous band, lateral extension of the base of the lacunar ligament along the pectineal line.

## 5. The rectus abdominis
- Paired muscle, long, flat, ribbon-like, extending vertically from the pubic symphysis to the costal margin, along the linea alba that separates the left and right rectus muscles.
- **Origin**: two tendinous heads — medial head (anterior surface of the pubic symphysis) and lateral head (lateral part of the pubic crest and pubic tubercle).
- **Insertion**: four fleshy digitations on the anterior thoracic wall, along a horizontal line passing laterally from the xiphoid, on the 5th, 6th and 7th costal cartilages.
- **Innervation**: the last five intercostal nerves and the subcostal nerve (T7-T12).
- **Action**: flexion of the trunk on the pelvis.

## 6. Pyramidalis muscle
- Rudimentary in humans; small triangular muscle, anterior to the lower part of the rectus abdominis, within its sheath. Base anterior to the pubis, apex directed superiorly and medially.
- **Origin**: anterior surface of the pubic body and anterior pubic ligament. **Insertion**: linea alba, midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis. **Innervation**: subcostal nerve (T12). **Action**: tenses the linea alba.

## 7. Functions of the anterior abdominal wall muscles
1. Provide resistant and extensible support for the abdominal viscera against gravity and protect them from trauma.
2. Compress the abdominal contents to increase intra-abdominal pressure, contributing to expulsive and expiratory acts.
3. Mobilize the trunk and maintain posture.

## 8. Trunk movements
- **Trunk flexion** (mainly lumbar): principally by the rectus abdominis.
- **Lateral flexion**: by unilateral contraction of the oblique muscles.
- **Rotation**: by combined contraction of the external oblique on one side and the internal oblique on the opposite side.

## 9. The rectus sheath
- Aponeurotic sheath enveloping the rectus abdominis (and pyramidalis if present), formed by the aponeuroses of the flat muscles of the anterior wall.
- **Anterior wall**: complete along the entire length of the muscle. **Posterior wall**: deficient below — presents a free border concave inferiorly, the **arcuate line (line of Douglas)**, between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis; below this level, the muscle rests directly on the transversalis fascia.
- **Above the arcuate line**: anterior wall = fusion of the external oblique aponeurosis with the anterior layer of the internal oblique aponeurosis; posterior wall = fusion of the transversus aponeurosis with the posterior layer of the internal oblique aponeurosis.
- **Below the arcuate line**: anterior wall = the three aponeuroses combined (transversus and internal oblique fused, external oblique separate); posterior wall deficient, formed solely by the transversalis fascia.
- **Contents of the rectus sheath**: 2 muscles (rectus abdominis and pyramidalis if present); 2 arteries (superior and inferior epigastric); 2 veins (superior and inferior epigastric); 6 nerves (terminal portions of the six last thoracic nerves, including the last five intercostal nerves and the subcostal nerve).

## Key points to remember
- Three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus) insert on the linea alba; their lower fibres form the conjoint tendon which reinforces the inguinal canal.
- The inguinal ligament is the thickened and rolled-up free inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis.
- The arcuate line (of Douglas) marks the limit below which the posterior wall of the rectus sheath disappears, leaving the muscle resting on the transversalis fascia.
- Segmental innervation T7-T12 (+L1 for internal oblique/transversus via iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal) for the entire wall.

# TP — Ostéologie du membre inférieur (s:
# Lab Practical — Osteology of the Lower Limb (Appendicular Skeleton)

## 1. Coxal Bone (Hip)
[[visual:anat/tp-hip-drawing]]
[[visual:anat/tp-hip-bone]]
- The coxal bone is a flat bone with **2 surfaces** (lateral or gluteal, with the acetabulum; medial, with the iliac fossa, auricular surface and symphyseal surface) and **4 borders**: **superior** (iliac crest), **anterior** (ASIS, AIIS, ilio-pubic eminence, pubis), **posterior** (PSIS, PIIS, greater ischial notch, ischial spine, lesser notch, tuberosity) and **inferior** (ischio-pubic ramus).
- Results from the fusion of 3 originally distinct bones at the level of the **cotyle (acetabulum)**: **ilium**, **ischium** and **pubis**.
- **How to distinguish the three bones**: the **ilium** is the wide wing **above** the acetabulum; the **ischium** is the **postero-inferior** part (tuberosity on which one sits); the **pubis** is the **antero-inferior** part that joins its counterpart at the symphysis. The ischium and pubis delimit the **obturator foramen** with their rami. The three bones are separated in the acetabulum by the **Y-cartilage**, ossified around 16 years of age.
- **Ilium**: superolateral part, presents the **iliac crest** (palpation landmark), the **anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)** and the **posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS)**.
- **Ischium**: postero-inferior part, presents the **ischial tuberosity** (weight-bearing surface in sitting position, insertion of the hamstring muscles) and the **ischial spine**.
- **Pubis**: antero-medial part, the two pubes unite at the **pubic symphysis**.
- **Greater ischial notch** and **lesser ischial notch**: separated by the ischial spine, allow passage of vascular-nervous structures (including the sciatic nerve through the greater notch).
- **Obturator foramen**: large antero-inferior opening, closed by the obturator membrane.
- **Acetabulum**: deep articular cavity receiving the femoral head (hip joint), formed by the contribution of the 3 bones.

## 2. Femur
[[visual:anat/tp-femur]]
- The longest and most solid bone in the body.
- **Femoral head**: spherical, bears the **fovea capitis** (insertion of the ligament of the femoral head, entry point for an accessory nutrient artery).
- **Femoral neck**: oblique, frequent site of fracture in the elderly (femoral neck fracture), zone with precarious vascularization.
- **Greater trochanter** and **lesser trochanter**: lateral and medial prominences, insertions of the pelvi-trochanteric muscles and psoas-iliacus respectively, connected by the **interthrochanteric line** (anterior) and the **interthrochanteric crest** (posterior).
- **Linea aspera**: longitudinal rough crest on the posterior surface of the shaft, insertion of numerous muscles (adductors, vastus lateralis/medialis).
- **Shaft**: 3 surfaces (anterior, medial, lateral) and 3 borders (medial, lateral, and posterior formed by the linea aspera with two ridges); it is convex anteriorly.
- Distal end: **medial condyle** and **lateral condyle**, separated posteriorly by the **intercondylar fossa**, **medial epicondyle** and **lateral epicondyle**, **patellar surface (femoral trochlea)** anteriorly.

## 3. Patella (Kneecap)
- The largest sesamoid bone in the body, embedded in the quadriceps tendon.
- Posterior articular surface, divided by a vertical ridge into two facets (medial and lateral) corresponding to the femoral trochlea.
- Base (proximal, wide) and apex (distal, pointed, giving insertion to the patellar ligament).

## 4. Tibia and Fibula (Bones of the Leg)
[[visual:anat/tp-leg-drawing]]
[[visual:anat/tp-leg-bones]]

### Tibia
- Medial bone of the leg, primary weight-bearing bone.
- Proximal end: **medial condyle** and **lateral condyle**, separated by the **intercondylar eminence (tibial spines)**; **tibial tuberosity** anteriorly (insertion of the patellar ligament).
- **Triangular** shaft: **3 surfaces** (**medial**, subcutaneous; **lateral**, in relation to the anterior compartment; **posterior**, with the soleal line) and **3 borders** (**anterior** or **tibial crest**, subcutaneous; **medial**; **interosseous**, lateral, for the interosseous membrane).
- Distal end: **medial malleolus**, articulating with the talus.

### Fibula (Peroneal Bone)
- Lateral bone, slender, non-weight-bearing (role of lateral stabilization and muscle insertion).
- **Fibular head** (proximal) articulates with the posterolateral surface of the lateral tibial condyle.
- Distal end: **lateral malleolus**, articulating with the talus, extends lower than the medial malleolus.
- Slender shaft with 3 surfaces (medial, lateral, posterior) and 3 borders (anterior, posterior, interosseous); the **interosseous membrane** unites it to the tibia.
- The common fibular nerve (common peroneal nerve, external popliteal nerve) winds around the fibular neck, superficial and vulnerable to trauma at this level.

## 5. Ankle (Talocrural Joint)
[[visual:anat/tp-ankle]]
- The **tibio-fibular mortise** is formed by the **tibial plafond** (inferior articular surface of the tibia), the **medial malleolus** (tibia) and the **lateral malleolus** (fibula), solidified by the **tibio-fibular syndesmosis**; it encloses the **talar trochlea**.
- The talar trochlea is wider anteriorly: the ankle is **more stable in dorsal flexion**.
- **Medial collateral ligament (deltoid)**: powerful, fan-shaped from the medial malleolus. **Lateral collateral ligament**: three bundles (anterior talo-fibular, calcaneo-fibular, posterior talo-fibular); the **anterior talo-fibular** is most often injured in inversion sprains.
- Below the ankle, the **subtalar joint** (talus-calcaneus) ensures inversion and eversion of the foot.

## 6. Tarsus and Foot Bones
[[visual:anat/tp-foot-medial]]
[[visual:anat/tp-foot]]
- Each tarsal bone has a **dorsal surface** (superior), a **plantar surface** (inferior) and articular surfaces; the **medial border** of the foot comprises the calcaneus, talus, navicular, medial cuneiform and metatarsal I, the **lateral border** the calcaneus, cuboid and metatarsal V.
- **Tarsus** (7 bones): **talus** (articulates with the tibia and fibula at the tibio-fibular mortise, transmits body weight to the foot), **calcaneus** (the most voluminous, forms the heel, insertion of the calcaneal tendon/Achilles tendon), **navicular**, **cuboid**, **medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms**.
- **Metatarsus**: 5 long bones (metatarsals I to V), proximal base, distal head.
- **Phalanges**: 3 per toe (proximal, middle, distal) except the hallux (great toe) which has only 2.
- The **plantar arches** (medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, transverse) distribute the mechanical stresses of the foot.

## Key Points for the Lab Practical
- Differentiate right/left femur based on the orientation of the head (medial) and the intercondylar fossa (posterior).
- Identify tibia versus fibula by size (the tibia is weight-bearing, robust; the fibula is slender) and the position of the malleoli (medial for the tibia, lateral and more distal for the fibula).
- Locate the 3 components of the coxal bone (ilium, ischium, pubis) and their convergence at the acetabulum.
- Associate each prominence with its function: trochanters and linea aspera (muscle insertions on the femur), tibial tuberosity (insertion of the patellar ligament), malleoli (ankle stability).
